claim: The study measured striatal dopamine synthesis capacity using [18F]-FDOPA PET in 94 healthy volunteers.
source: We measured striatal dopamine synthesis capacity using [18F]-FDOPA PET in a large sample of healthy volunteers (N = 94)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sample size and imaging method used.

claim: None of the trait measures (working memory capacity, trait impulsivity, sEBR, subjective reward sensitivity) correlated significantly with striatal dopamine synthesis capacity.
source: None of these trait measures correlated significantly with striatal dopamine synthesis capacity, nor did they have out-of-sample predictive power.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the main finding of no significant correlations.

claim: Bayes factor analyses indicated evidence in favor of absence of correlations for all trait measures except subjective reward sensitivity.
source: Bayes factor analyses indicated the evidence was in favour of absence of correlations for all but subjective reward sensitivity.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the Bayesian analysis results.

claim: The mesocorticolimbic dopamine system plays a key role in cognitive control processes including working memory.
source: The mesocorticolimbic dopamine system plays a key role in a range of cognitive functions, including cognitive control processes, such as working memory (Arnsten and Li, 2005)
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Individual differences in striatal dopamine function have been associated with working memory capacity, impulsivity, and spontaneous eye-blink rate.
source: individual differences in striatal dopamine function have been associated with various behavioural and physiological trait characteristics, including working memory capacity, impulsivity, and spontaneous eye-blink rate (sEBR)
evidence: The statement summarizes prior research findings mentioned in the introduction.

claim: Working memory capacity is positively associated with striatal dopamine synthesis capacity according to some PET studies.
source: evidence from work with brain positron emission tomography (PET) in humans indicates that working memory capacity is positively associated with both striatal dopamine synthesis capacity, assessed with 6-[18F]fluoro-l-m-tyrosine ([18F]-FMT) PET imaging, and striatal dopamine release, estimated with [11C]-raclopride PET imaging (Bäckman et al., 2011; Clatworthy et al., 2009; Cools et al., 2008; Landau et al., 2009; Salami et al., 2019; but see Braskie et al., 2008, Braskie et al., 2011; Klostermann et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior PET studies.

claim: Greater dopamine synthesis or release in the caudate nucleus is associated with improved updating of working memory.
source: These studies observed that greater dopamine synthesis or release, typically in the caudate nucleus, was associated with improved updating of working memory in particular (Bäckman et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Unmedicated patients with Parkinson's disease show striatal underactivation and impaired performance during working memory updating.
source: The PET findings are also corroborated by studies with unmedicated patients with Parkinson's disease that show striatal underactivation and impaired performance during working memory updating (Marklund et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a patient study.

claim: Lesions of the caudate nucleus cause impairment of working memory performance in experimental animals.
source: as well as from experimental animal work demonstrating that lesions of the caudate nucleus cause impairment of working memory performance (Collins et al., 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to animal research.

claim: Impulsivity is positively correlated with striatal dopamine release, synthesis capacity, and D2-receptor availability according to PET studies.
source: Work with PET imaging in human volunteers has also demonstrated a positive correlation between impulsivity and both striatal dopamine release and synthesis capacity as well as striatal dopamine D2-receptor availability (Buckholtz et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2014; van Holst et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple PET studies.

claim: Parkinson's disease patients who developed treatment-induced impulse control disorders had reduced striatal dopamine transporter availability and increased dopamine release in the ventral striatum.
source: This is supported by evidence from a meta-analysis showing that patients with Parkinson's disease who developed treatment-induced impulse control disorders had reduced striatal dopamine transporter availability and increased dopamine release in the ventral striatum in response to reward-related stimuli (Martini et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a meta-analysis.

claim: Individual variation in sEBR correlates with working memory task performance.
source: Individual variation in sEBR has been found to correlate with working memory task performance (Ortega et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: sEBR correlates with working memory updating and gating.
source: Individual variation in sEBR has been found to correlate with working memory task performance (Ortega et al., 2022), working memory updating and gating (Rac-Lubashevsky et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: sEBR has been argued to be an effective measure of striatal dopamine activity.
source: Given such findings, it has been argued that sEBR is an effective measure of striatal dopamine activity (Jongkees and Colzato, 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review or theoretical paper.

claim: Positive correlations exist between sEBR and dopamine D2-receptor availability throughout the striatum.
source: The notion is supported, however, by positive correlations between sEBR and dopamine D2-receptor availability throughout the striatum (Groman et al., 2014; but see Dang et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research, with a contrasting citation also noted.

claim: sEBR correlates with post-mortem dopamine concentrations in the caudate nucleus of monkeys.
source: as well as post-mortem dopamine concentrations in the caudate nucleus of monkeys (Taylor et al., 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to animal research.

claim: Simple off-the-shelf tests have been suggested as approximations of striatal dopamine activity instead of expensive PET imaging.
source: Findings like these have raised the suggestion that instead of requiring invasive and expensive brain PET imaging, we can approximate striatal dopamine activity with relatively simple, off-the-shelf tests, for example, the digit span or listening span tests of working memory capacity (Cools et al., 2008; Landau et al., 2009), eye-blink rate measurements at rest (Jongkees and Colzato, 2016), or self-report measures of relevant traits such as impulsivity or reward sensitivity (Buckholtz et al., 2010; Clatworthy et al., 2009; Depue and Collins, 1999; Froböse et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The predictive value of working memory capacity, trait impulsivity, and sEBR for individual variation in striatal dopamine function has not yet been established.
source: However, the predictive value of working memory capacity, trait impulsivity, and sEBR for individual variation in striatal dopamine function in the human brain has not yet been established.
evidence: The statement identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Sample sizes of prior studies may have produced inflated and unstable estimates of correlation coefficients.
source: In fact, sample sizes of prior studies of these measures have been so small that they might well have produced inflated and unstable estimates of the correlation coefficient (Loken and Gelman, 2017; Schönbrodt and Perugini, 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to methodological literature on sample size effects.

claim: Cools et al., 2008 and Landau et al., 2009 reported positive correlations between working memory capacity and dopamine synthesis capacity.
source: For example, although both Cools et al., 2008 and Landau et al., 2009 (N = 11 and N = 22, respectively) reported a positive correlation between working memory capacity, measured with the listening span, and dopamine synthesis capacity
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to specific prior studies.

claim: Subsequent studies using partly overlapping samples did not find the relationship between working memory capacity and dopamine synthesis capacity.
source: subsequent studies using a partly overlapping sample did not find this relationship (Braskie et al., 2011; Braskie et al., 2008; Klostermann et al., 2012; all using subsets from one sample of N = 37 participants, of which 20 overlapped with Landau et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to specific studies with sample overlap information.

claim: Trait impulsivity has been observed to correlate negatively rather than positively with striatal dopamine levels, synthesis capacity, and D2-receptor availability in some studies.
source: Similarly, trait impulsivity has also been observed to correlate negatively rather than positively with striatal dopamine levels, synthesis capacity, and D2-receptor availability (Dalley et al., 2007; Martinez et al., 2020; Petzold et al., 2019, N = 60; Smith et al., 2016, N = 16)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies showing opposite direction of correlation.

claim: Sescousse et al., 2018 reported evidence for the absence of a correlation between sEBR and striatal dopamine synthesis capacity.
source: Furthermore, Sescousse et al., 2018 reported evidence for the absence of a correlation between sEBR and striatal dopamine synthesis capacity (N = 30)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Dang et al., 2017 found a lack of correlation between sEBR and dopamine D2-receptor availability.
source: similar to the lack of a correlation between sEBR and dopamine D2-receptor availability (N = 20) observed by Dang et al., 2017
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: The striatum is a functionally heterogeneous structure with distinct connectionist anatomy with the cortex.
source: The subcortical dopamine system is not a single entity and the striatum is a functionally heterogeneous structure with a distinct connectionist anatomy with the cortex, involving a functional gradient in the connections between the cortex and ventral striatum (primarily nucleus accumbens), dorsolateral striatum (putamen), and dorsomedial striatum (caudate nucleus; Alexander et al., 1986; Haber et al., 2000; Joel and Weiner, 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to neuroanatomical literature.

claim: The study performed analyses in three striatal regions of interest: caudate nucleus, putamen, and nucleus accumbens.
source: we performed our analyses in three striatal regions of interest (ROIs), defined using a parcellation based on intra-striatal functional connectivity in an independent sample (Piray et al., 2017). The ROIs approximately matched the anatomical subdivision of the striatum into caudate nucleus, putamen, and nucleus accumbens (ventral striatum).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the ROI approach used in the analysis.

claim: There were no significant correlations between dopamine synthesis capacity in any of the three striatal ROIs and working memory capacity, trait impulsivity, or sEBR, even without correcting for multiple comparisons.
source: There were no significant correlations between dopamine synthesis capacity, in any of the three striatal ROIs, and working memory capacity, trait impulsivity, or sEBR, even without correcting for multiple comparisons (Figure 1, Table 1; all uncorrected p-values>0.050, all corrected p-values≥0.365)
evidence: The results section explicitly states the statistical findings with p-values.

claim: There was no significant correlation between subjective reward sensitivity and dopamine synthesis capacity after correction for multiple comparisons.
source: There was also no significant correlation with subjective reward sensitivity after correction for multiple comparisons (Figure 1, Table 1; corrected p-values=0.127)
evidence: The results section explicitly states the statistical finding with p-value.

claim: The correlation coefficients between dopamine synthesis capacity and both Digit Span and Listening Span were almost zero in all three ROIs.
source: Specifically, the coefficients of correlation between dopamine synthesis capacity and both the Digit Span and Listening Span were almost zero in all three ROIs (Figure 1a and b, Table 1)
evidence: The results section explicitly describes the magnitude of correlation coefficients.

claim: The direction of the association between Digit Span and dopamine synthesis capacity was negative (ρ=–0.071 for the nucleus accumbens).
source: In fact, the direction of the association between Digit Span and dopamine synthesis capacity was negative (e.g. ρ=–0.071 for the nucleus accumbens)
evidence: The results section explicitly provides the correlation coefficient value.

claim: The coefficient of correlation between trait impulsivity and dopamine synthesis capacity was almost zero in all three ROIs, with a negative direction if anything.
source: The coefficient of the correlation between trait impulsivity and dopamine synthesis capacity was also almost zero in all three ROIs, and the direction of the association was, if anything, negative (Figure 1c, Table 1)
evidence: The results section explicitly describes the correlation coefficients.

claim: Correlation coefficients between sEBR and dopamine synthesis capacity were almost zero in the caudate nucleus and putamen, with a positive but non-significant association in the nucleus accumbens (ρ=0.123).
source: There were also no significant correlations between sEBR and dopamine synthesis capacity (Figure 1d, Table 1), with correlation coefficients of almost zero in the caudate nucleus and putamen, and a positive (but non-significant) association in the nucleus accumbens (ρ=0.123)
evidence: The results section explicitly provides correlation coefficient values.

claim: Subjective reward sensitivity was most strongly and positively associated with dopamine synthesis capacity among the four trait measures (ρ=0.179 in the nucleus accumbens), but the correlations were not statistically significant.
source: Among the four trait measures under consideration, subjective reward sensitivity was most strongly and positively associated with dopamine synthesis capacity (e.g. ρ=0.179 in the nucleus accumbens), but again the correlations were not statistically significant (Figure 1e, Table 1)
evidence: The results section explicitly provides correlation coefficient values and statistical significance.

claim: Voxel-wise regression analyses did not reveal any significant clusters for the trait measures on dopamine synthesis capacity.
source: In accordance with the ROI-based correlation analyses, voxel-wise regression analyses of the trait measures on the dopamine synthesis capacity PET data did not reveal any significant clusters
evidence: The results section explicitly states the voxel-wise analysis findings.

claim: For working memory capacity measured with Digit Span, the data were approximately 10-12 times more likely under the null hypothesis of no positive correlation than under the alternative hypothesis of a positive correlation.
source: For working memory capacity, the BF01 results indicated that the data were approximately 10–12 times more likely under the null hypothesis of no positive correlation than under the alternative hypothesis of a positive correlation for the Digit Span
evidence: The results section explicitly provides Bayes factor values.

claim: For working memory capacity measured with Listening Span, the data were approximately 6 times more likely under the null hypothesis than under the alternative hypothesis of a positive correlation.
source: and approximately 6 times more likely under the null hypothesis for the Listening Span, thus providing strong evidence for H0 over H1 for the Digit Span and moderate evidence for the Listening Span
evidence: The results section explicitly provides Bayes factor values and interpretation.

claim: There was strong evidence for the null hypothesis of no positive correlation between trait impulsivity and dopamine synthesis capacity (BF01 ≈ 5–8).
source: Similarly, there was strong evidence for the null hypothesis of no positive correlation between trait impulsivity and dopamine synthesis capacity (BF01 ≈ 5–8)
evidence: The results section explicitly provides Bayes factor values and interpretation.

claim: For sEBR, there was moderate evidence for the null hypothesis of no positive correlation with dopamine synthesis capacity in the caudate nucleus and putamen (BF01 ≈ 6), but only weak, inconclusive evidence in the nucleus accumbens (BF01 ≈ 2).
source: For sEBR, the analysis revealed moderate evidence for the null hypothesis of no positive correlation with dopamine synthesis capacity in the caudate nucleus and putamen (BF01 ≈ 6), but only weak, inconclusive evidence in the nucleus accumbens (BF01 ≈ 2)
evidence: The results section explicitly provides Bayes factor values and interpretation.

claim: The data for the correlation between subjective reward sensitivity and dopamine synthesis capacity were equally likely under the null or alternative hypothesis (BF01 ≈ 1), indicating inconclusive Bayesian analysis.
source: The data for the correlation between subjective reward sensitivity and dopamine synthesis capacity were equally likely under H0 or H1 (BF01 ≈ 1), indicating that the Bayesian analysis was inconclusive about the evidence for the existence of a positive correlation
evidence: The results section explicitly provides Bayes factor values and interpretation.

claim: For all trait measures, the cross-validated R² was negative for dopamine synthesis capacity in all three striatal ROIs.
source: For all trait measures, the cross-validated R2 was negative for dopamine synthesis capacity in the caudate nucleus, putamen, and nucleus accumbens ROIs (Table 2)
evidence: The results section explicitly states the cross-validation findings.

claim: Using a trait measure to predict dopamine synthesis capacity resulted in worse performance than simply predicting the average dopamine synthesis capacity.
source: This implies that using a trait measure to predict dopamine synthesis capacity resulted in a worse performance than simply predicting the average dopamine synthesis capacity – in other words, ignoring individual differences altogether
evidence: The results section explicitly interprets the negative R² values.

claim: Permutation testing indicated that for all trait measures the cross-validated predictive performance was not statistically significant (all permutation p-values >0.10).
source: Permutation testing indicated that for all trait measures the cross-validated predictive performance was not statistically significant (Table 2; all permutation p-values >0.10)
evidence: The results section explicitly provides permutation test p-values.

claim: The study provides evidence for a lack of correlations between striatal dopamine synthesis capacity and simple off-the-shelf tests of working memory capacity, trait impulsivity, sEBR, and subjective reward sensitivity.
source: In this study, we provide evidence for a lack of correlations between striatal dopamine synthesis capacity, measured with [18F]-FDOPA PET imaging, and simple, off-the-shelf tests of working memory capacity, trait impulsivity, sEBR, and subjective reward sensitivity
evidence: The discussion section explicitly summarizes the main finding.

claim: Bayes factor analyses provided evidence in favor of the absence of correlations, except for the BAS questionnaire, for which the evidence was inconclusive.
source: Bayes factor analyses provided evidence in favour of the absence of correlations, except for the BAS questionnaire, for which the evidence was inconclusive
evidence: The discussion section explicitly summarizes the Bayesian analysis findings.

claim: Cross-validation analyses revealed little out-of-sample predictive power of each trait measure for dopamine synthesis capacity.
source: Furthermore, cross-validation analyses revealed little out-of-sample predictive power of each trait measure for dopamine synthesis capacity
evidence: The discussion section explicitly summarizes the cross-validation findings.

claim: The study's sample size was more than adequate to reliably detect effects of magnitudes previously observed in smaller-scale studies.
source: However, our sample size was more than adequate to reliably detect the effects of magnitudes that were previously observed, as the previous smaller-scale studies reported coefficients of 0.6 or higher for the correlations between dopamine synthesis capacity and working memory capacity (Cools et al., 2008; Landau et al., 2009) and impulsive behaviour (van Holst et al., 2018), as well as between direct measures of caudate nucleus dopamine levels and sEBR (Taylor et al., 1999)
evidence: The discussion section explicitly compares the current sample size to prior studies and their effect sizes.

claim: The absence of correlations was not due to measurement error in the estimates of striatal dopamine synthesis capacity or a lack of behavioral relevance of these estimates.
source: Critically, the absence of correlations was not due to measurement error in the estimates of striatal dopamine synthesis capacity or a lack of behavioural relevance of these estimates
evidence: The discussion section explicitly addresses potential alternative explanations.

claim: Dopamine synthesis capacity in this dataset has been shown to account for effort-based decision-making, response vigour, reversal learning, and smartphone social activity in the expected direction.
source: dopamine synthesis capacity in this dataset has been shown to account for (dopamine drug effects on) effort-based decision-making, response vigour, reversal learning, and smartphone social activity in the expected direction (Hofmans et al., 2020; Hofmans et al., 2022; van den Bosch et al., 2022; Westbrook et al., 2020; Westbrook et al., 2021)
evidence: The discussion section cites multiple studies using the same dataset showing behavioral relevance.

claim: [18F]-FDOPA uptake in the striatum was associated positively with the value of cognitive effort.
source: More specifically, [18F]-FDOPA uptake in the striatum was associated positively with the value of cognitive effort (Hofmans et al., 2020; Westbrook et al., 2020; both with N = 46)
evidence: The discussion section cites specific studies showing associations with cognitive effort.

claim: [18F]-FDOPA uptake in the striatum was associated with the impact of average reward value on response vigour.
source: with the impact of average reward value on response vigour (Hofmans et al., 2022; N = 44)
evidence: The discussion section cites a specific study showing associations with response vigour.

claim: [18F]-FDOPA uptake in the striatum was associated with dopaminergic drug-related changes in prediction error-related BOLD signal in the striatum.
source: and with dopaminergic drug-related changes in prediction error-related BOLD signal in the striatum (van den Bosch et al., 2022; N = 85)
evidence: The discussion section cites a specific study showing associations with prediction error signals.

claim: More sophisticated and quantitative indices of value-based learning, motivation, and daily logs of social activity might be better proxy measures of striatal dopamine synthesis capacity than the simple trait measures.
source: The implication of this body of work is that more sophisticated and quantitative indices of value-based learning, motivation, and even daily logs of participants' social activity on their smartphone (Westbrook et al., 2021; N = 22) might be better proxy measures of striatal dopamine synthesis capacity than the simple trait measures reported here
evidence: The discussion section explicitly suggests alternative approaches based on prior findings.

claim: The present results speak specifically of the relationship of the trait measures with striatal dopamine synthesis capacity and do not speak of the presence or absence of correlations with other aspects of the dopamine system.
source: It should be noted that the present results speak specifically of the relationship of the trait measures with striatal dopamine synthesis capacity. They do not speak of the presence or absence of correlations with other aspects of the dopamine system, such as dopamine D2/3-receptor availability or dopamine release
evidence: The discussion section explicitly limits the scope of the findings.

claim: Working memory, trait impulsivity, and sEBR have all been associated with D2/3-receptor availability and/or dopamine release.
source: Indeed, working memory, trait impulsivity, and sEBR have all been associated with D2/3-receptor availability and/or dopamine release (Bäckman et al., 2011; Buckholtz et al., 2010; Clatworthy et al., 2009; Garrett et al., 2022; Groman et al., 2014; Jongkees and Colzato, 2016; Kim et al., 2014), although the results for impulsivity and sEBR are mixed (Dang et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2009)
evidence: The discussion section cites multiple studies showing associations with other dopamine measures.

claim: Recent large-scale studies have demonstrated crucial involvement of both striatal and extrastriatal dopamine D2/3-receptor availability in working memory performance using PET-fMRI measures.
source: Recent large-scale studies have demonstrated crucial involvement of both striatal and extrastriatal dopamine D2/3-receptor availability in working memory performance using PET-fMRI measures (Garrett et al., 2022; Salami et al., 2019)
evidence: The discussion section cites recent studies on receptor availability and working memory.

claim: Only prefrontal and not striatal receptor availability was significantly different between low and normal working memory groups.
source: but only prefrontal and not striatal receptor availability was significantly different between low and normal working memory groups (Salami et al., 2018)
evidence: The discussion section cites a specific study showing regional differences.

claim: A large-scale SPECT study in healthy volunteers (N = 188) did not find evidence for significant relationships between striatal dopamine transporter availability and working memory performance or trait impulsivity.
source: One such large-scale SPECT study in healthy volunteers (N = 188) did not find evidence for significant relationships between striatal dopamine transporter availability and working memory performance or trait impulsivity, in line with the current results for striatal dopamine synthesis capacity (Burke et al., 2011)
evidence: The discussion section cites a large SPECT study with findings consistent with the current results.

claim: In one study, striatal dopamine synthesis capacity was found to correlate negatively with dopamine D2/3-receptor availability.
source: In one such study, striatal dopamine synthesis capacity, as indexed by L-[β-11C]-DOPA PET imaging, was found to correlate negatively with dopamine D2/3-receptor availability, as indexed with [11C]raclopride (Ito et al., 2011; N = 14)
evidence: The discussion section cites a specific study showing negative correlation between synthesis capacity and receptor availability.

claim: Some studies found no relationship between dopamine synthesis capacity and D2/3-receptor availability.
source: but no relationship was observed in others (Heinz et al., 2005; Kienast et al., 2008; Yamamoto et al., 2021; N = 24, 12, and 29, respectively)
evidence: The discussion section cites multiple studies showing no relationship.

claim: A recent study (N = 40) using [18F]-FMT found striatal dopamine synthesis capacity to be positively correlated with striatal dopamine D2/3-receptor availability but not with striatal dopamine release.
source: Conversely, another recent study (N = 40) that used [18F]-FMT found striatal dopamine synthesis capacity to be positively correlated with striatal dopamine D2/3-receptor availability but not with striatal dopamine release (Berry et al., 2018)
evidence: The discussion section cites a specific study showing positive correlation with receptor availability.

claim: Trait measures of working memory capacity, trait impulsivity, and sEBR have frequently been found to account for individual differences in the cognitive effects of dopaminergic drugs.
source: The trait measures of working memory capacity, trait impulsivity, and sEBR have frequently been found to account for individual differences in the cognitive effects of dopaminergic drugs, for example, in the domain of reinforcement learning and Pavlovian biasing of instrumental action (Cavanagh et al., 2014; Cools et al., 2003; Cools et al., 2007; Frank and O'Reilly, 2006; Froböse et al., 2018; Rostami Kandroodi et al., 2021; Kimberg et al., 1997; Mehta et al., 2000; van der Schaaf et al., 2014)
evidence: The discussion section cites multiple studies showing trait-dependent drug effects.

claim: The present results do not invalidate previous findings of trait-dependent effects of dopamine drugs but raise the hypothesis that these effects reflect other factors than individual variation in baseline dopamine synthesis capacity.
source: We emphasize that the present results do not invalidate these previous findings but raise the hypothesis that the interactive effects between dopamine drug effects and trait characteristics reflect other factors than individual variation in baseline dopamine synthesis capacity
evidence: The discussion section explicitly interprets the implications of the findings.

claim: Dopaminergic drugs might have different effects on reinforcement learning in people with low and high working memory capacity because of differences in the degree to which the drugs boost reinforcement learning or working memory strategies for task performance.
source: For example, dopaminergic drugs might have different effects on reinforcement learning in people with low and high working memory capacity because of differences in the degree to which the drugs boost reinforcement learning or working memory strategies for task performance (Collins, 2018; Collins et al., 2014)
evidence: The discussion section provides an alternative explanation supported by citations.

claim: The absence of correlations observed in this study provides a cautionary message for future studies that may be tempted to use these behavioral indices as a proxy for striatal dopamine synthesis capacity.
source: The absence of such correlations observed here provides a strong cautionary message for future studies that may be tempted to use these relatively simple behavioural indices of working memory capacity, trait impulsivity, sEBR, or subjective reward sensitivity as a proxy for striatal dopamine synthesis capacity
evidence: The conclusion explicitly states the main implication of the findings.

claim: 100 healthy volunteers were recruited for the larger project, 50 women and 50 men (age at inclusion: range 18–43, mean [SD] = 23.0 [5.0] y).
source: This study is part of a larger project (Määttä et al., 2021) for which 100 healthy volunteers were recruited, 50 women and 50 men (age at inclusion: range 18–43, mean [SD] = 23.0 [5.0] y)
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the participant sample.

claim: Six participants dropped out before completion of the study, resulting in PET data available for 94 participants.
source: Six participants dropped out before completion of the study because of discomfort in the MRI or PET scanner (N = 4), personal reasons (N = 1), or technical failure of the PET scanner (N = 1). Therefore, PET data were available for a total of N = 94 participants
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes participant attrition.

claim: For the sEBR analyses, the final sample was N = 92 after exclusions.
source: For the sEBR analyses, one participant was excluded due to poor data quality and one was excluded as an outlier (more than 5 SDs from the group mean), resulting in a final sample of N = 92
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes sample size for sEBR analyses.

claim: For the impulsivity analyses, the final sample was N = 66.
source: For the impulsivity analyses, 67 participants completed the BIS-11 questionnaire (see subsection 'Trait impulsivity' for details), one of whom was excluded due to missing PET data, resulting in a final sample of N = 66
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes sample size for impulsivity analyses.

claim: The study employed a within-subject, placebo-controlled, double-blind cross-over design.
source: Data were collected as part of a large PET, pharmaco-fMRI study on the effects of methylphenidate and sulpiride on brain and cognition, employing a within-subject, placebo-controlled, double-blind cross-over design
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the study design.

claim: The study consisted of five testing days separated by at least 1 week.
source: The study consisted of five testing days separated by at least 1 wk
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the testing schedule.

claim: Participants received 150 mg of carbidopa and 400 mg of entacapone 50 minutes before the PET scan to minimize peripheral metabolism of [18F]-FDOPA.
source: 50 min before the PET scan started, participants received 150 mg of carbidopa and 400 mg of entacapone to minimize peripheral metabolism of [18F]-FDOPA by peripheral decarboxylase and catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT), respectively, thereby increasing signal-to-noise ratio in the brain (Boyes et al., 1986; Hoffman et al., 1992; Ishikawa et al., 1996; Léger et al., 1998)
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the pharmacological preparation for PET scanning.

claim: [18F]-FDOPA is a substrate for aromatic amino acid decarboxylase, the enzyme that converts DOPA into dopamine.
source: The tracer is a substrate for aromatic amino acid decarboxylase, the enzyme that converts DOPA into dopamine
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the mechanism of the tracer.

claim: The rate of conversion of [18F]-FDOPA into dopamine provides an estimate of dopamine synthesis capacity.
source: The rate of conversion of [18F]-FDOPA into dopamine provides an estimate of dopamine synthesis capacity
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes what the tracer measures.

claim: [18F]-FDOPA is a stable measure with good test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficients range from about 0.7–0.94 in the striatum).
source: It is a stable measure with good test–retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficients range from about 0.7–0.94 in the striatum) even after a 2-yr time interval between acquisitions of scans (Egerton et al., 2010; Vingerhoets et al., 1994)
evidence: The methods section cites studies demonstrating the reliability of the measure.

claim: Dynamic PET data were acquired over 89 minutes and divided into 24 frames.
source: Dynamic PET data (4 × 4 × 3 mm voxel size; 5 mm slice thickness; 200 × 200 × 75 matrix) were acquired over 89 min and divided into 24 frames (4 × 1, 3 × 2, 3 × 3, 14 × 5 min)
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the PET acquisition parameters.

claim: Presynaptic dopamine synthesis capacity was quantified as the tracer influx rate kicer (min–1) per voxel using Gjedde–Patlak modelling.
source: Presynaptic dopamine synthesis capacity was quantified as the tracer influx rate kicer (min–1) per voxel with graphical analysis for irreversible tracer binding using Gjedde–Patlak modelling (Patlak and Blasberg, 1985; Patlak et al., 1983)
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the quantification method with citations.

claim: The kicer values represent the rate of tracer accumulation relative to the reference region of cerebellar grey matter.
source: The kicer values represent the rate of tracer accumulation relative to the reference region of cerebellar grey matter, where the density of dopamine receptors and metabolites is extremely low compared to the striatum (Farde et al., 1986; Hall et al., 1999)
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the reference region with citations.

claim: Working memory capacity was indexed with the Digit Span test and Listening Span test.
source: Working memory capacity was indexed with the Digit Span test (Groth-Marnat, 1997) and Listening Span test (Daneman and Carpenter, 1980)
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the working memory measures.

claim: The Digit Span test consists of forward and backward sections where participants repeat series of numbers.
source: In the Digit Span test, participants started with the forward section, in which they listened to a series of numbers and were required to repeat the correct numbers in order. The series increased in length (starting at three digits) until the participant failed two attempts on a series length, or until the maximum length of nine digits was completed. Next, in the backwards section, participants again listened to a series of numbers but were required to repeat the correct numbers in reverse order
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the Digit Span task procedure.

claim: The Digit Span was performed twice, once on the intake session and once on the final testing day, with test-retest correlation of ρ = 0.8.
source: The Digit Span was performed twice, once on the intake session and once on the final testing day, before the PET scan (test–retest correlation: ρ = 0.8)
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the test-retest reliability.

claim: Trait impulsivity was assessed with the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11).
source: Trait impulsivity was assessed with the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11; Patton et al., 1995)
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the impulsivity measure.

claim: The BIS-11 is a self-report questionnaire consisting of 30 statements about common (non)impulsive behaviors and preferences.
